title: Leg 61 — Cheyenne Plains to Kimball
subtitle: Cheyenne, Frontier Days, missile country and the Lodgepole corridor
preflightBriefing: Welcome aboard. We are leaving Northern Colorado Regional and heading north across the plains toward Cheyenne, then east along the old transportation corridor toward Pine Bluffs and Kimball. Around Cheyenne I will keep the visual order tight: after waypoint two, F. E. Warren Air Force Base, Frontier Park, the state-capitol area and the Union Pacific district all lie off the left side in that order as we turn east. Frontier Park itself is several miles from the route and may be hard to pick out, so I will not oversell it as an obvious landmark. Farther east the story shifts to missile country, the railroad, the Lincoln Highway and the Lodgepole Creek corridor before we finish at Kimball. I'll stay quiet while you taxi and depart. Once you're airborne and settled, say Trip continue.

waypoints.name: Cheyenne Frontier Days Pass
viewingNotes: After the eastbound turn, Cheyenne's major city sights lie generally off the left side. Frontier Park is several miles north of the route and small-site detail may be scenery-dependent.

waypoints.name: Lodgepole Creek Exit
viewingNotes: Pine Bluffs lies north of the route near this point; the route continues east toward the Nebraska line and Kimball.

blocks.title: Leaving northern Colorado
blocks.text: We are leaving the Loveland and Fort Collins area and heading north across the open Front Range plains. The Rockies stay well off to the left while the ground below becomes more agricultural and less urban. This is the same broad north-south corridor we used on the previous leg, but today we are peeling away from the mountains and toward the high plains.

blocks.title: The high plains open up
blocks.text: The country below is part of the High Plains: broad, windy, comparatively dry and shaped as much by grassland and agriculture as by towns. From the air, the straight roads and field boundaries can make the landscape look almost engineered, but water availability and wind still decide a great deal about where people can farm and settle.

blocks.title: Back into Wyoming
blocks.text: We are crossing back into Wyoming now. There is no dramatic geographic boundary here; the same plains continue north. What changes is the historical pull of Cheyenne ahead, a city whose location was chosen largely because the Union Pacific needed a workable route across the mountains to the west.

blocks.title: Cheyenne ahead
blocks.text: Cheyenne is beginning to come into the broader view ahead. Surveyor Grenville Dodge selected the site near Crow Creek in 1867 for the Union Pacific, and the railroad arrived that November. The town grew so quickly that it earned the nickname Magic City of the Plains.

blocks.title: Approaching the Cheyenne turn
blocks.text: We are coming up the south side of Cheyenne now. The city itself sits mostly ahead and to the right during this northbound stretch. After waypoint two we will turn east, and the main Cheyenne sights will then line up off the left side in a much more useful viewing order.

blocks.title: A city built around the railroad
blocks.text: Cheyenne never became just another temporary end-of-track camp. The Union Pacific made it an important operational center, and by the late nineteenth century major shops and yards were established here. The railroad's need for powerful locomotives on nearby Sherman Hill later made Cheyenne a home base for some of the largest steam engines ever used in regular service.

blocks.title: The Cheyenne eastbound turn
blocks.text: Waypoint two is coming up. Once we turn east, keep your attention mainly to the left. The next several miles contain the most concentrated Cheyenne material on this leg, and I will call the sights in the order the airplane encounters them rather than jumping around the city.

blocks.title: F. E. Warren off the left
blocks.spokenLabel: F. E. Warren Air Force Base
blocks.text: Just after the turn, F. E. Warren Air Force Base lies off the left side. It began in 1867 as Fort D. A. Russell, created to protect workers building the Union Pacific. Today it is the oldest continuously active military installation in the Air Force and home to the 90th Missile Wing, which operates 150 Minuteman Three intercontinental ballistic missiles.

blocks.title: Frontier Park farther left
blocks.text: Farther off the left side is Frontier Park, roughly several miles north of our route. The grandstand is not a large target from this altitude, so do not expect it to jump out of the scenery. The event began in 1897 after a Union Pacific passenger agent proposed a festival celebrating cowboy skills. It grew into Cheyenne Frontier Days, the Daddy of 'em All. Buffalo Bill brought his Wild West show alongside the second celebration, and decades later Cheyenne-raised rodeo champion and singer Chris LeDoux both competed here and returned as a concert headliner.

blocks.title: Capitol and depot district
blocks.text: Central Cheyenne is also off the left now. The state-capitol area sits north of downtown, while the Union Pacific depot is farther south near the tracks. The depot, completed in the 1880s from sandstone quarried near Fort Collins, became one of the grand landmarks of the transcontinental railroad and remains a National Historic Landmark.

blocks.title: Cheyenne and the Big Boys
blocks.text: Cheyenne's railroad story has a spectacular mechanical side. The steep grades west of the city demanded enormous locomotives, and Cheyenne became a maintenance base for Union Pacific's Challengers and Big Boys. Only twenty-five Big Boys were built. Number 4014, restored to operating condition, is based here at the Union Pacific steam shop.

blocks.title: A quiet-looking nuclear landscape
blocks.text: As Cheyenne falls behind, the open country becomes part of one of the most unusual landscapes in America. F. E. Warren's missile field spreads across portions of Wyoming, Nebraska and Colorado. The launch facilities are intentionally dispersed and visually modest, so a landscape that looks almost empty from the cockpit is also part of the nation's active strategic nuclear deterrent.

blocks.title: The old east-west corridor
blocks.text: We are moving toward the Lodgepole Creek corridor, one of the practical routes travelers used across this part of the plains. An eastern branch of the Overland Trail followed Lodgepole Creek, and the Union Pacific later used much the same general line. U.S. 30 and the Lincoln Highway also inherited parts of this transportation geography.

blocks.title: Pine Bluffs to the left
blocks.text: Pine Bluffs is coming up off the left side near the Wyoming-Nebraska line. It sits along the old Lincoln Highway and Union Pacific corridor. The local Texas Trail Museum preserves that transportation and ranching history with a Union Pacific caboose, a covered wagon, an early schoolhouse and collections from the surrounding high plains.

blocks.title: Into Nebraska
blocks.text: We are leaving Wyoming and entering the Nebraska Panhandle. The terrain does not change abruptly, but the route is now settling into the long east-west Lodgepole Creek valley that helped guide railroads, roads and communities across this dry part of the plains.

blocks.title: Why towns formed along the tracks
blocks.text: Steam railroads needed water, maintenance points and crews at regular intervals, so tiny settlements appeared along the Union Pacific line. Some grew and some disappeared, but the railroad imposed a repeating human rhythm on a landscape where natural water sources and older trails had already shaped movement.

blocks.title: Cold War infrastructure under the prairie
blocks.text: The Cold War added another layer to this corridor. Atlas missiles were the first operational American intercontinental ballistic missiles, but they were complicated liquid-fueled weapons and were soon replaced by solid-fueled Minuteman missiles. The plains around southeastern Wyoming and western Nebraska became ideal missile country because launch sites could be widely dispersed across open land.

blocks.title: Kimball ahead-left
blocks.text: Kimball is now the next town ahead and slightly left of our airport course. The airport lies south of town, so we will reach the runway before flying directly over the community. Kimball began around 1870 as a Union Pacific water and worker stop called Antelopeville, then took the name Kimball in 1885 for railroad executive Thomas Lord Kimball.

blocks.title: Oil, missiles and a sudden population boom
blocks.text: Kimball had a remarkable second growth spurt in the twentieth century. Oil was discovered in 1951, and within a decade the town's population nearly tripled. Then missile construction arrived. An Atlas site was dug south of town, followed by construction activity for dozens of Minuteman launch sites across the region, bringing another wave of workers, housing and public-service demands.

blocks.title: A hotel and an Eisenhower connection
blocks.text: One of Kimball's more human-scale stories is the old Wheat Growers Hotel, built in 1918 and promoted as a glamorous stop between Omaha and Denver. Dwight and Mamie Eisenhower stayed there with family in 1919, the same year Eisenhower took part in the Army's famous transcontinental motor convoy.

blocks.title: Kimball Municipal Airport
blocks.text: Kimball Municipal Airport is just ahead. The town itself remains a few miles to the left and north of the field, so this is another case where the destination airport arrives before the community center. Today's leg has followed a remarkably persistent corridor: military roads, railroad, highway, missile fields and modern aviation all layered across the same open plains.
